notes: MCP-stub-backed suite (see evals/lib/mcp-stub), with a fake GitHub (evals/lib/github-fixture.py) for the preferences and rubric evals. The executor is a real, separate `claude -p --strict-mcp-config` subprocess run by evals/lib/run-mcp-trials.sh; triage's own run-trials.sh is a thin caller of it. Triage presents one item per reply and applies each answer before the next item, so every eval is a conversation: evals with a `follow_ups` key script the user's replies (an empty list marks a single-turn eval whose last question the user must not answer: 1 and 5), and every other eval is played by the simulated user, briefed through its `simulated_user` string. Run the whole suite in one command with SIMULATED_USER=1: `TRIALS_DIR="$TMPDIR/triage-trials" SIMULATED_USER=1 bash plugins/life-skills/skills/triage/evals/run-trials.sh`. The top-level "instruction_files": "managed-only" keeps the running user's own instructions out of every trial (the driver's private HOME drops ~/.claude/rules but not an AGENTS.md above the workspace); keep TRIALS_DIR under $TMPDIR all the same. transcript.txt separates turns with `===== turn N =====`, conversation.txt holds both sides of a simulated-user run, and tools.log records each call's turn, which is how expectations such as 'no write in turn 1' or 'the label is created after the offer' are graded. Evals 1-3, 10, 13, 17, 18, 22, 25, 33, and 36 cover the Trello path; 4-6, 11, 12, 19-21, 24, 31, 32, and 34 the email workflow (Step 7b) and capture to Trello (Step 7c); 7-9, 14, 15, 26-30, 35, 37, and 38 the Jira path via the Atlassian stub. Evals 13-16 and 28 cover the processing order (Step 1b), with Trello `pos` and Jira `rank` values the stubs order by but never return; 16 asks the order question first. Evals 17-21 cover following links and naming the user's own action (Steps 5a and 6); their URLs use the reserved .invalid top-level domain. 21-23 cover the safety and consent rules: instructions inside fetched content, a request that authorizes nothing, and a sole candidate found after an open answer to the scope question. Evals 24-38 cover a capture that finds an existing card, passed deadlines, staleness bands, a bulk-import timestamp, two order signals disagreeing, duplicates on a professional project, Tier 2 and Tier 3, the delete branch, an account without Action or Waiting For labels (32, converted from the removed label bootstrap to 'existing labels only'), auto-captured placeholder content, two open boards, duplicates found per item (35, converted from the removed up-front batch proposals to Step 4 and the Step 9b offer), an item that leaves scope mid-run, a new arrival, and the stall interview (38, which stages conduct-interview). Eval 11 likewise now grades the similar-items offer in place of an up-front batch archive. Evals 39-54 cover the one-item-per-reply rewrite: one item per reply on Gmail (39), Trello under up-front authorization (40), and Jira (41); a pattern label offered once for three items (42) and not for two (43); sift-email's rubric read from a verified private checkout and a contradicting label flagged (44); archive versus complete on Trello (45), with Gmail read state in 39 and 50; the preferences file found by an owner-limited search and applied without asking (46), not found with nothing written (47), a stated default saved on a yes (48), and a public or another user's repository skipped (49); the similar-items offer (50) and 'apply this to any others like it' with a near-miss (51); an image-only email body (52); and triage recording rather than doing the work (53) against a lookup the user asked for (54). Evals 55-58 add a quick lookup that fills a gap in the item itself (55), a linked guide in a repository the user can't open (56), 'apply this to any others like it' on Gmail with a near-miss (57), and a default stated mid-run saved to an existing preferences file while a one-off decision is not (58). Evals 36 and 37 use the stubs' scheduled_changes, which apply someone else's write partway through a trial; those writes are part of the final state but are not the skill's. Every eval whose correct run can write carries a final expectation that the conversation's account of its changes matches the final state in both directions. Every fixture names an anchor_date, and evals/lib/fixture-dates.py moves its dates to the run date in whole weeks; dates in prose, here and in the fixtures, are {{date:...}} tokens. Grade against each trial's resolved eval.json, <service>-state-seed.json, github-seed.json, and github-state-out.json, not this file and the raw fixtures.
